title: Price marking and overcharging
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
summary: Traders must display prices for goods and may not sell above the marked or controlled price.
keyPoints: Prices must be clearly displayed
Selling above the marked price is an offence
Complaints can be made to the Consumer Affairs Authority
penalty: Fines and, in some cases, imprisonment under the Act. Verify current amounts.
example: A shop charges Rs. 50 above the printed price on a packet. You can complain to the CAA hotline 1977.

title: Rights over defective goods
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
summary: Consumers can seek a remedy when goods or services are defective or not as described.
keyPoints: Keep your receipt as proof
Ask for a repair, replacement or refund
Escalate to the CAA if the seller refuses
penalty: Remedies depend on the case: refund, replacement, or CAA action against the trader.
example: A phone stops working in two days. Show the receipt and request a replacement or refund.

title: Carrying a valid driving licence
summary: A driver must hold a valid licence for the class of vehicle and produce it when asked by police.
keyPoints: Licence must match the vehicle class
Carry the licence and vehicle documents
Expired or missing licences can lead to fines
penalty: Fine on conviction or on-the-spot fine procedure. Verify current amounts.
example: A police officer stops you at a checkpoint and asks for your licence. You must present it.

title: Drink driving
summary: Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs is a serious offence.
keyPoints: Police may test drivers
Licence can be suspended
Applies to all vehicle types
penalty: Fine, imprisonment, and possible licence suspension or disqualification.
example: A driver is tested after a minor collision and found over the limit. He can be charged in court.

title: EPF and ETF contributions
act: Employees' Provident Fund Act No. 15 of 1958 and Employees' Trust Fund Act No. 46 of 1980
summary: Employers must contribute to the EPF and ETF for eligible employees.
keyPoints: Employer contributes 12% to EPF and employee 8%
Employer contributes 3% to ETF
You can check your balance with the Central Bank / ETF Board
penalty: Employers who fail to pay can face surcharges and legal action by the Labour Department.
example: Your employer deducts EPF from your salary but does not remit it. You can complain to the Labour Department.

title: Maternity leave
summary: Women employees are entitled to paid maternity leave.
keyPoints: 84 working days for the first two living children
Shorter period for later children
Employer must not dismiss for pregnancy
penalty: Employers who breach it can be prosecuted. Verify details for your sector.
example: A private-sector employee is denied leave for her second child. She can report to the Labour Department.

title: Transfer of land requires a notarial deed
act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
summary: A sale or transfer of land must be in writing and executed before a Notary Public and witnesses.
keyPoints: Verbal agreements are not enough
Register the deed at the Land Registry
Check the title before buying
penalty: An improperly executed transfer may be invalid and unenforceable.
example: A buyer pays for land on a handwritten note only. The transfer is at risk of being void without a notarial deed.

title: Ownership by long possession
summary: Uninterrupted and adverse possession of immovable property for ten years can give rights of ownership.
keyPoints: Possession must be continuous and without the owner's consent
Applies to immovable property
A court must usually declare the title
penalty: No penalty. The remedy is a court declaration of title.
example: A family farms a plot openly for over ten years while the owner never objects. They may claim title by prescription.

title: Unauthorized access to computers
summary: Accessing a computer or account without authority is a criminal offence.
keyPoints: Hacking and password theft are covered
Spreading data obtained illegally is an offence
Report to the police or SL CERT
penalty: Fine and imprisonment depending on the offence.
example: A student logs into a friend's social media account without permission and posts messages. This may be an offence.

title: Personal data rights
act: Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022
summary: Individuals have rights over how organizations collect and use their personal data.
keyPoints: Right to access your data
Right to correct inaccurate data
Organizations must process data lawfully
penalty: Penalties are imposed by the Data Protection Authority. Check implementation status.
example: A company collects your details for one purpose and sells them. You can complain to the authority.

title: Maintenance for spouse and children
summary: Parents and spouses may be required to provide financial maintenance, claimed in the Magistrate's Court.
keyPoints: Children are entitled to maintenance
Application is made to the Magistrate's Court
Court sets the amount based on needs and means
penalty: Non-payment of a court order can lead to enforcement and imprisonment.
example: A father stops supporting his child after separation. The mother can apply for a maintenance order.

title: Protection from domestic violence
act: Prevention of Domestic Violence Act No. 34 of 2005
summary: Victims of domestic violence can apply for a protection order from the Magistrate's Court.
keyPoints: Covers physical and emotional harm
Protection orders can bar the abuser from the home
Police can assist in urgent situations
penalty: Breach of a protection order is an offence leading to fine or imprisonment.
example: A woman is repeatedly threatened at home. She can approach the police or court for a protection order.

title: Right to Information
act: Right to Information Act No. 12 of 2016
summary: Citizens can request information held by public authorities.
keyPoints: Submit a written request to the Information Officer
A response is due within 14 working days
Appeal to the RTI Commission if refused
penalty: Officers who refuse without a valid reason may face penalties.
example: You request details of a public school's fund use. The authority must respond or give a lawful reason.

title: Helmets for motorcyclists
act: Motor Traffic Act No. 14 of 1951 and its regulations
summary: Riders and pillion passengers on motorcycles must wear a protective helmet.
keyPoints: Applies to the rider and the pillion passenger
The helmet must be worn properly
Police can fine riders without a helmet
penalty: Fine on conviction. Verify the current amount.
example: A rider is stopped at a checkpoint without a helmet. He can be fined.

title: Misleading advertisements
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
summary: Traders must not use false or misleading claims when advertising or selling goods and services.
keyPoints: Claims about quality, price or origin must be true
Consumers can complain to the Consumer Affairs Authority
Keep a copy or photo of the advertisement as evidence
penalty: Penalties under the Act, which may include fines. Verify current amounts.
example: A shop advertises a 50% discount but the item was never sold at the higher price. You can complain to the CAA.

title: Expiry dates and unsafe food
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003 and Food Act No. 26 of 1980
summary: Packaged food must carry proper labelling, and selling expired or unfit food is an offence.
keyPoints: Check the manufacture and expiry dates before buying
Food sold must be fit for human consumption
Report to the Public Health Inspector or the CAA
penalty: Fines or imprisonment under the Acts, depending on the offence. Verify current amounts.
example: You find expired biscuits on a shop shelf. You can report the shop to the Public Health Inspector.

title: Seat belts
act: Motor Traffic Act No. 14 of 1951 and its regulations
summary: Seat belts are required for people in the front seats of motor cars, and the rules can extend to other seats.
keyPoints: Driver and front passenger must wear a seat belt
Rules can change, so check current regulations
Children should be properly restrained
penalty: Fine on conviction. Verify the current amount and rules.
example: A driver is stopped by police with the front passenger not wearing a seat belt. Both may be fined.

title: Using a mobile phone while driving
act: Motor Traffic Act No. 14 of 1951 and its regulations
summary: Using a hand-held mobile phone while driving is prohibited because it distracts the driver.
keyPoints: Hands-free use is treated differently, so check the rule
Applies to cars, motorcycles and other vehicles
Pull over safely to use the phone
penalty: Fine on conviction. Verify the current amount.
example: A bus driver is seen holding a phone to his ear while driving. He can be fined.

title: Duty after a road accident
summary: A driver involved in an accident must stop, help any injured person and report to the police.
keyPoints: Do not leave the scene
Give your details to the other party and the police
Report the accident at the nearest police station
penalty: Failing to stop or report is an offence leading to fine or imprisonment.
example: A motorist hits a pedestrian lightly and drives away. This is a serious offence.

title: Gratuity
act: Payment of Gratuity Act No. 12 of 1983
summary: Employees who complete five years of continuous service are entitled to gratuity when they leave the job.
keyPoints: Minimum five years of service
Calculated as half a month's wage for each year of service
Applies to workplaces covered by the Act
penalty: Employers who refuse to pay can be pursued through the Labour Department.
example: A worker resigns after eight years and the employer refuses to pay. He can complain to the Labour Department.

title: Termination of employment
act: Termination of Employment of Workmen (Special Provisions) Act No. 45 of 1971
summary: Employers of a certain size cannot terminate workers freely and need the worker's consent or approval from the Commissioner of Labour.
keyPoints: Applies to larger employers, so check the threshold in the Act
A worker can complain to the Labour Department
Possible remedy is reinstatement or compensation
penalty: Remedies are ordered by the Commissioner of Labour or the Labour Tribunal.
example: A factory worker is dismissed without notice or reason. He can complain to the Labour Department.

title: Sexual harassment at work
summary: Sexual harassment, including unwelcome sexual comments or touching, is a criminal offence.
keyPoints: Applies in workplaces and public places
Report to the police and to your employer
Keep records of messages and incidents
penalty: Imprisonment and/or fine, and the court may order compensation. Verify details.
example: A manager repeatedly sends inappropriate messages to a junior colleague. She can complain to the police.

title: Rights of tenants
summary: A landlord cannot simply throw a tenant out. Eviction needs a lawful process through the courts.
keyPoints: Keep rent receipts and the written agreement
The Act covers certain premises, so check coverage
A court order is usually required for eviction
penalty: The remedy is through the courts. Illegal eviction can lead to legal action.
example: A landlord changes the locks while the tenant is at work. The tenant can seek legal advice and go to court.

title: Registering a deed
summary: Deeds about land should be registered at the Land Registry to protect the buyer's rights.
keyPoints: Registration protects your priority over later buyers
Use the correct folio and extent when registering
Always get a title search done before buying
penalty: No penalty. Failing to register can cost you your rights to the land.
example: Two people are sold the same land by one seller. The deed registered first usually has priority.

title: Electronic documents and signatures
summary: Electronic records and electronic signatures can be legally valid, like paper documents.
keyPoints: Supports online contracts and e-records
Keep digital copies as evidence
Some documents may still need paper form
penalty: No direct penalty. The Act gives legal recognition to electronic transactions.
example: You accept a work offer by email. The email can serve as evidence of the agreement.

title: Copyright and copying work
summary: Original works such as writing, software and music are protected, and copying them without permission is infringement.
keyPoints: Copyright arises automatically when a work is created
Credit and permission matter when using others' work
Applies to software and online content
penalty: Civil remedies and criminal penalties under the Act. Verify details.
example: A student copies another student's software project and submits it as his own. This can be copyright infringement.

title: Registering a marriage
summary: Under the general law, marriages must be registered, and the minimum age to marry is 18. Muslim marriages follow the Muslim Marriage and Divorce Act.
keyPoints: A marriage certificate is proof of marriage
Registration is done through the Registrar
Different laws apply to different communities
penalty: A marriage that breaks the legal requirements may be invalid. Verify details.
example: A couple completes a ceremony but never registers. They may later struggle to prove the marriage.

title: Compulsory education
summary: Children between the ages of 5 and 14 are required to attend school.
keyPoints: Parents are responsible for sending children to school
Free education is provided in government schools
Report out-of-school children to the Education Office
penalty: Parents who fail to comply can face action under the law. Verify details.
example: A 10-year-old is kept at home to work. The family can be directed to ensure school attendance.

title: Rights when arrested
summary: A person who is arrested has the right to be told the reason and to be brought before a judge according to law.
keyPoints: You have the right to know why you are arrested
You must be produced before a judge as required by law
You have the right to a lawyer of your choice
penalty: Unlawful arrest or detention can be challenged in court.
example: A man is held at a police station for days with no explanation. His family can seek help from a lawyer.

title: Petitioning for fundamental rights
summary: If a fundamental right is infringed by the State, a person can petition the Supreme Court, usually within one month.
keyPoints: Applies to actions by the State or its officers
The time limit is short, so act quickly
A lawyer's help is strongly advised
penalty: The Supreme Court can grant relief and compensation.
example: A public officer unlawfully refuses a person's rights. The person can file a petition within one month.
